title: Data-efficient reconstruction of critical quantum dynamics via blind fractional-envelope extrapolation
authors: Hyunju Kim, Hyun-Yong Lee, Heung-Sik Kim
abstract: Simulating real-time dynamics of quantum systems is often limited to short times by entanglement growth. Finite-pole reconstructions such as linear prediction and related machineries extrapolate such data reliably when the spectrum is a finite set of excitations, but at criticality the low-energy spectrum is a power-law continuum $A(ω)\sim|ω|^{α-1}$ -- a branch cut whose real-time tail $G(t)\sim t^{-α}$ finitely many poles cannot represent. Here we develop a fractional-calculus-motivated envelope extrapolation for such data. Its structure is motivated by a fractional form of Schwinger--Dyson (fSD) equation, in which the Laplace symbol $s^α$ carries the branch cut analytically while the residual self-energy remains meromorphic. On real data we employ the corresponding operational alternative -- the exponent $α$ is selected blindly inside the fit window, the signal is detrended by $t^α$, the residual is fitted by a stabilized finite-pole model, and the algebraic envelope is restored. On the critical XXZ chain this blind fractional-envelope method (fSD for short) extrapolates short-time data typically several-fold more accurately than finite-pole methods, with the exponent $α$ identified blindly from the fit window alone and bracketing the closed-form Luttinger value at weak coupling. The same blind search finds the $z=2$ dilute-magnon exponent $α=1/2$ at the $Δ=1$ saturation transition, and the advantage persists in the gapped free-magnon phase with its sharp band edges. On noncritical dynamical mean-field spectra, whose low-frequency response is regular, fSD by contrast fails to select any stable fractional envelope and reduces to the standard pole result rather than manufacturing a spurious power law, making it an efficient and accurate route to quantum critical dynamics when only short simulation times are accessible.
summary: This work introduces a novel fractional envelope extrapolation method (fSD) designed to overcome the limitations of simulating quantum dynamics at criticality. By treating the low-energy spectrum as a branch cut rather than discrete poles, the technique accurately reconstructs long-time decay tails from short simulation data. This is particularly valuable for studying strongly correlated electron models and critical phenomena.
main_problem: Simulating real-time dynamics of quantum systems is limited by entanglement growth, especially at criticality where the spectrum exhibits a power-law continuum.
main_result: A fractional-calculus-motivated envelope extrapolation method (fSD) accurately reconstructs short-time critical dynamics, significantly outperforming standard finite-pole methods.
method: The technique involves blind selection of the critical exponent $\alpha$, detrending the signal by $t^\alpha$, fitting the residual with a stable finite-pole model, and then restoring the algebraic envelope.
model_or_system: The method is tested on quantum systems exhibiting criticality, including the XXZ spin chain and the single-orbital Hubbard model studied via Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT).
key_observables: Real-time correlation functions $G(t)$, spectral function $A(\omega)$, and the critical exponent $\alpha$.
important_parameters: The critical exponent $\alpha$, system parameters like magnetic field ($h$) or interaction ratios ($U/D$), and time windows for fitting.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the low-energy physics is dominated by a power-law continuum $t^{-\alpha}$ at criticality, allowing the use of fractional calculus techniques.
figures_summary: Figures compare fSD extrapolation against finite-pole methods on critical chains (XXZ), showing superior agreement with theoretical tails; other figures track exponent $\alpha$ across varying fields or show spectral function resolution in DMFT transitions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the failure of standard pole fitting at criticality, introduces the fSD framework based on fractional calculus, details the operational procedure (blind search), and validates it by comparing results against known critical points and non-critical regimes.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, data-driven tool to extract long-time dynamical information from short numerical simulations in strongly correlated systems where standard spectral analysis fails due to power-law continua.
